To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a new method for the automated classification of tailed phages and that we have used it to assign a large number of new phage genomes to our classification system.
we developed a computational method to automatically identify the head, neck and tails proteins of tailed phages and assign them to a classification of morphological subfamillies.
we developed a method that can automatically classify most taided phages and that this method is able to assign a function to the majority of their structural module genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of computational methods and tools for the classification and analysis of tailed bacterophages.
a better understanding of phage diversity and the evolution of their virion architecture.
the identification and classification of phages based upon the structure of their head-neck-tail complex, a feature that can be inferred from the sequences of their genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach provides a robust and efficient method for the automatic classification of tailed phages according to their head-neck-tail architecture.
the diversity of phages is not only limited by the number of possible structural solutions for the head-neck-tail organization but also by the limited number of solutions used by nature.
our classification of tailed phages is consistent with the morphological classification and that the latter can be used to predict the former.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can automatically classify most taided bacteriophages based on neck proteins and assign a function to the head, neck and tails genes.
the neck is a major component of the virion structure, which is used in a limited number of ways to produce functional tailed phages.
the neck of tailed phages is more conserved than the head and tail, and that this conservation is reflected in a consistent set of neck proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diversity of the neck proteins in tailed phages is not as large as previously thought and that the neck organization is a key element for phage classification.
the diversity of phage neck proteins is much lower than previously assumed and that only a limited set of neck proteins is used to connect the phage head and tail.
the structural module is highly conserved in tailed phages.
